content.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
The Antarctica presents the coldest (temperatures between –25 °C
and –89 °C), driest (average RH 0.03%), and windiest (chilly all-year
Katabatic winds averaging 15-50 km/h) environment on Earth - a continent
at the highest average elevation (2300 m above MSL). Due to its extreme
weather system, and unique geo-location around the South Pole, it is one of
the last frontiers for the human race. Medical research in recent years has
focused on the life-style of Antarctic expeditionary members, exposed to
harsh environmental and psychological conditions over a prolonged period
of time [1]. The Antarctic milieu comes with extreme cold, intense UV
radiation, white-outs, varying magnetic fields, sleep deprivation, altered cir-
cadian biorhythms, memory loss, and isolation - causing significant physi-
ological and psychological stresses [2-4].
The Antarctic stations offer a unique research environment, as these
stations built in Antarctica provide simulated environment to prepare space
crews for their missions [5], to study atmospheric, geological and biomedi-
cal research sciences as an analogue of space on earth [6]. These stations
also simulate the typical environment in submarines, and underwater habi-
tats and provide a real-life and real-time observations of human behavior
and experience similar to the aforementioned conditions. The cold, dry, and
radiation conditions, as well as difficulty in getting external support in re-
mote areas in Antarctica where various stations are situated, also simulate
the conditions prevailing in Mars [7, 8]. Thus each research station pro-
vides a unique environment [1, 9], and offer advantages to study human
physiological, immunological and behavioral health in natural setting [3].
The visiting population is fit; usually young, consumes the same diet,
experiences the same environment, isolated from the rest of the world for

long periods, and is subjected to great seasonal differences in temperature
and sunlight in terms of light and dark cycles [10, 11]. Medical records
show that Antarctica is a comparatively healthier place to live. However,
healthy, transient populations who 'winter' in Antarctica, generally come
from the densely populated regions, and suddenly get confined to this ex-
treme environment [10]. The wintering expeditioners are totally physically
isolated for periods of 8 to 13 months [12, 13]. Such population remains
away from pollution and other health affecting agents such as infectious
organism and parasites [14-16]. Many people expect medical research in
Antarctica to be about cold resistance. However, while there is continuing
interest in this topic, the real opportunity in Antarctic biomedical research
lies on evaluation of human physiology in isolated environments [17- 20].
Although, few reports are available on psychology, physiology, endocrinol-
ogy, chronobiology, and epidemiological studies [3], and changes have been
observed in various body systems. However, the effect of such stringent
conditions on immune system of expeditioners during short and long term
stay in Antarctica have not been explored much. Hence the present study
was undertaken to evaluate the immunological changes in Indian Antarctic
expeditioners.
Defence Institute of Physiology & Allied Sciences (DIPAS) has con-
ducted Immunological, Biochemical,  Proteomic and Metabolic studies, on
two teams of Indian Antarctic expeditioners who were the participants of
28th Indian Scientific Antarctic Expedition from December 2008 to De-
cember 2009. The participants from summer team (Jan 2009 to March
2009), were exposed to acute stress while the participants from wintering
team (Jan 2009 to Dec 2009), were exposed to chronic stress.  The inves-
tigations were carried out to observe the effect of multiple stresses like
ship journey, isolation, cold, magnetic field and UV exposure, on human
immune responses. For both short and long term exposure study, sera and
saliva samples were collected at different stages of the expedition. The
parameters analysed for immunological studies were cytokines, chemokines,
and Immunoglobulins, Stress markers Netrin-1, soluble HLA-G , cortisol,
Leptin and catecholamine. In addition, for biochemical studies, parameters
like glucose, cholesterol, triglycerides, SGPT, SGOT, Alkaline phosphatase
and Creatinine were measured. Numerous low-Molecular weight metabo-
lites in serum, including lactate, creatine, succinate, glucose, glycoproteins,
LDL, 3 hydroxy butyrate, tri-methylamine N-oxide (TMAO), and various
